passages.text: CHIN-COUGH, or HOOPING-COUGH, a convulsive cough, in which the patient, after several quick expirations, draws in his breath with a loud and shrill noise, called the hoop.
It is chiefly a disease of children, and is very contagious; it seldom attacks the same person a second time.
It commonly lasts many weeks, and sometimes several months; and it proves dangerous chiefly to infants, and when it is joined with inflammation of the lungs.
The disease is supposed to arise from a peculiar contagion, which acts upon the nerves of the lungs and stomach, and brings on fits of coughing that often end in vomiting.
The cure is attempted by gentle vomits, frequently repeated, and by blisters between the shoulders; and in the later stage, by the bark and by opiates.
A change of air is found to be of great service; and riding on horseback or in a carriage has been much recommended.
Whooping cough, also known as pertussis or the 100-day cough, is a highly contagious bacterial disease caused by Bordetella pertussis.
After one or two weeks of cold-like symptoms, severe coughing fits begin. A fit may end with a high-pitched whoop as the person breathes in, and vomiting after coughing is common.
The coughing may last for ten weeks or more.
The disease is most dangerous in babies. Pneumonia is a common complication and cause of death.
Neither infection nor vaccination gives lifelong immunity. Protection wanes over the years, and adults can catch the disease again.
The pertussis vaccine prevents the disease. It is given to infants in combination with diphtheria and tetanus vaccines.
Antibiotics such as azithromycin shorten the time a person is contagious. Given early, they may also make the illness milder.

reasons: The old headword CHIN-COUGH differs from the modern title, but the entry names it HOOPING-COUGH.
Both texts describe the coughing fits, the whoop and the danger to infants.
Bordetella pertussis scores lower because it covers the bacterium more than the disease.

alignments.label: The whoop

britannica.quote: draws in his breath with a loud and shrill noise, called the hoop

wikipedia.quote: a high-pitched whoop as the person breathes in

alignments.note: Same sign. Change in language only.

alignments.label: Only once

britannica.quote: it seldom attacks the same person a second time

alignments.note: Infection gives protection, but it does not last for life. Adults can catch the disease again.

alignments.label: Danger to infants

britannica.quote: it proves dangerous chiefly to infants

alignments.note: Same fact. Both also name lung inflammation, now pneumonia.

alignments.label: Cause

britannica.quote: a peculiar contagion, which acts upon the nerves of the lungs

alignments.note: A contagion is right, and a bacterium is that contagion. The action on the nerves is wrong.

alignments.label: Vomits and blisters

britannica.quote: The cure is attempted by gentle vomits

alignments.note: Change in knowledge. Vomits and blisters do not treat the infection.

alignments.label: Change of air

britannica.quote: riding on horseback or in a carriage has been much recommended

alignments.note: Wikipedia does not list a change of air or riding as a treatment. Inference: the advice has no effect on the infection.

alignments.label: Vaccine

wikipedia.quote: The pertussis vaccine prevents the disease

alignments.note: The vaccine came in the 20th century. The 1810 text has no means of prevention.

suggestedQuestions: Can a person catch whooping cough twice?
What did the 1810 entry recommend as a cure?

Can a person catch whooping cough twice?.answer: The 1810 entry says it seldom attacks the same person a second time [B2]. Wikipedia says neither infection nor vaccination gives lifelong immunity, so adults can catch it again [W5].

What did the 1810 entry recommend as a c.answer: Gentle vomits, blisters between the shoulders, and later the bark and opiates [B5], plus a change of air and riding [B6]. Wikipedia lists antibiotics such as azithromycin [W7] and prevention by vaccine [W6].
